Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.

summaries.gardner: Lowe's is a well-known, profitable incumbent in a mature industry, not a Rule Breaker: it is the number-two player behind Home Depot, its market is not emerging, and the shares have fallen about 20% over the past year. It fails most of Gardner's traits apart from brand recognition.
summaries.buffett: Lowe's is a simple, understandable business with a long dividend record and high returns on capital, and it has shrunk its diluted share count from 750 million (FY2020) to 560 million (FY2025). Against that, it is the weaker of two duopolists, carries $37.6B of debt with a shareholders' deficit, and earnings have drifted down since FY2023, so it fits Buffett's checklist only in part.
summaries.munger: Munger would value the simple duopoly economics and the efficient-scale barrier, but would note that Lowe's is structurally second to Home Depot, relies on debt-funded buybacks, and is tied to the housing cycle. At about 16-17 times earnings it is a fair-price good business rather than a wonderful one.
summaries.lynch: In Lynch's categories Lowe's is a stalwart with a simple story (more Pro, online and services sales, plus a housing recovery), and the shares are down near 52-week lows. But a P/E around 16-17 against single-digit expected earnings growth gives a PEG well above 1, so it is not a Lynch bargain.
summaries.fisher: Fisher looked for companies with long sales runways driven by innovation and outstanding sales organisations; Lowe's has a capable management team and good cost control but little R&D and a mature market. It fits only partly, mainly on management quality and selling skill.
summaries.graham: Lowe's passes Graham's size, ten-year profitability and 20-year dividend tests, and EPS rose from $7.75 (FY2020) to $11.85 (FY2025). It fails on balance-sheet strength (debt far above cash, negative book value), and its P/E of about 16 on three-year average earnings is slightly above his 15 limit.
summaries.thiel: Lowe's has no proprietary technology, no monopoly and no secret, so it answers few of Thiel's seven questions well. Its strengths are distribution (1,759 stores) and durability, not a 10x better product.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner favours companies with accelerating growth riding big platform shifts at reasonable prices; Lowe's has flat comparable sales, falling margins and no secular tailwind, though it is profitable and generates solid free cash flow. It fits poorly.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller looks for accelerating earnings and a supportive macro backdrop; Lowe's estimates have been cut, guidance was lowered to the bottom of its range in August 2026, and high mortgage rates hold back housing. A falling-rate housing recovery could be a future catalyst, but the setup is not yet in place.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith wants high returns on capital without leverage, high gross margins and growth; Lowe's earns a high ROIC (about 22%) but only because years of debt-funded buybacks left negative equity, and its 33% gross margin and flat organic sales are ordinary. It is a decent business, not a Fundsmith-style compounder.
summaries.greenblatt: On Greenblatt's Magic Formula, Lowe's has a high return on capital and an earnings yield (EBIT to enterprise value) of roughly 7%, which is reasonable but not deeply cheap. It would likely rank in the middle to upper part of a large-cap screen.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool asks for a great business, talented and honest management, and the ability to reinvest at high returns. Lowe's has a solid business and competent management, but limited high-return reinvestment opportunities, so it has returned most cash through dividends and buybacks and is now spending $10B on acquisitions with uncertain returns.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for simple businesses in temporary distress bought with low downside; Lowe's is simple and its housing-related slump looks cyclical, but at about 16-17 times earnings the price is not a 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' bargain, and leverage adds risk.
summaries.wood: Lowe's is not an innovation-platform company in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomics, and its market will not multiply in five years. It does not fit ARK's disruptive-innovation framework.
summaries.ackman: Ackman seeks simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and high barriers; Lowe's is simple, predictable over the cycle and cash generative ($7.7B FCF in FY2025), but is not dominant and is highly leveraged. It fits partly, more as a cyclical-recovery idea than a core holding.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep favoured scale-economics-shared businesses that keep passing savings to customers; Lowe's has scale but does not visibly reinvest its savings into lower prices, and in July 2026 it declined to match rivals' price cuts. It does not fit the Nomad model.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed young companies attacking huge, fast-growing markets with new technology; Lowe's is a decades-old retailer in a mature market. It does not fit his approach.
summaries.nash: Lowe's fails most of Tom Nash's hard filters: revenue growth below 10%, operating margin below 20%, much more debt than cash, and no secular trend. Its Nash scorecard total of about 50 out of 130 falls well short of the 75 threshold, and a Nash-style DCF at a 12% discount rate gives a value far below the share price.

momentum.evidence: The shares closed at $197.38 on Oct 16, 2026, down about 20% over 52 weeks and near a 52-week low, while the S&P 500 rose.

g4.evidence: CEO Marvin Ellison is a seasoned retail operator, and institutions own about 80% of the shares, but no famous investor or strategic partner is a notable backer.

g6.evidence: Commentators mostly describe Lowe's as cyclically pressured rather than overvalued; the consensus price target is $252 against a $197 price.

simple.evidence: Lowe's sells home improvement goods and services from about 1,759 US stores and online, a business any generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: It has been profitable for decades and raised its dividend for more than 25 consecutive years, but sales fell from $97.1B (FY2022) to $83.7B (FY2024) and net earnings from $8.4B (FY2021) to $6.7B (FY2025).

integrity.evidence: Management is candid in guidance (it cut FY2026 guidance to the low end in August 2026) and pay is tied to results, but heavy debt-funded buybacks drove shareholders' equity to a deficit, a debatable capital choice.

b6.evidence: Lowe's largely mirrored Home Depot's push into Pro distribution, buying FBM ($8.8B) and ADG (~$1.3B) in 2025 after Home Depot bought SRS, which looks partly like copying the leader.

roic.evidence: Return on invested capital is about 22%, but it is flattered by debt: Lowe's carries $37.6B of debt and a $7.4B shareholders' deficit.

fcf.evidence: FY2025 operating cash flow of $9,864M minus capex of $2,213M gave free cash flow of $7,651M, 115% of net earnings of $6,654M.

b10.evidence: Most retained cash went into buybacks that cut diluted shares from 750M to 560M and lifted EPS from $7.75 to $11.85 (FY2020-FY2025), but the share price is now lower than in 2021, so market value has not kept pace.

safety.evidence: A conservative DCF of free cash flow (about $7.7B a year, low growth) less $34B of net debt gives a value well below the $197 share price.

fairprice.evidence: At about 16-17 times trailing earnings and a 6-7% free-cash-flow yield, the price is reasonable for a mature duopolist but not cheap given flat organic growth and high leverage.

mu5.evidence: The duopoly position makes outright failure unlikely, but high leverage, housing-cycle exposure and a larger competitor are real ways for value to erode.

reinvest.evidence: Store growth is minimal and capex is only about $2.2-2.5B a year, so Lowe's mostly returns cash or buys businesses rather than reinvesting at high returns.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart with a simple story: gain Pro, online and home services share and benefit when housing turnover recovers.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 16.7 is far above expected EPS growth of roughly 5-6% for FY2027.

runway.evidence: Growth depends on Pro distribution (FBM, ADG), online and services in a roughly $1 trillion market, but the store base is mature and the company is US-only.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares fell from 750M (FY2020) to 560M (FY2025), but buybacks were nearly paused in FY2025 ($211M) after the acquisitions, and no notable insider buying was found.

ly8.evidence: Lowe's is a widely followed mega-cap covered by about 35 analysts.

fi2.evidence: Management keeps adding new offers (Pro distribution, home services, retail media, online marketplace), but these are business-model extensions rather than new products.

fi3.evidence: Lowe's does not disclose R&D spending; its technology investment goes into e-commerce, supply chain and store systems.

fi4.evidence: Online sales grew 15.7% and Pro and home services drove five straight positive comp quarters through Q2 2026, but Home Depot remains the stronger seller to Pros.

longterm.evidence: Lowe's made multi-year investments in its supply chain and spent about $10.1B on acquisitions in FY2025 for Pro growth, while also prioritising buybacks and EPS targets.

gr1.evidence: Lowe's had FY2025 sales of $86.3B and a market value of about $110B.

ni10.evidence: Lowe's has been profitable in every one of the last ten years, earning $6.7B in FY2025.

gr4.evidence: Lowe's has paid a quarterly dividend without interruption since its 1961 IPO and has raised it for more than 25 consecutive years (to $1.25 in 2026).

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $7.75 in FY2020 to $11.85 in FY2025, more than one-third in just five years.

gr6.evidence: The price is about 15.9 times average diluted EPS of the last three years ($13.20, $12.23, $11.85), just above Graham's 15 limit.

gr7.evidence: Book value is negative (a $7.4B shareholders' deficit at July 31, 2026), so the P/E × P/B test cannot be met.

th1.evidence: Lowe's has no proprietary technology that is ten times better than rivals; it sells largely the same products as Home Depot.

timing.evidence: High mortgage rates, low home turnover and cautious DIY spending made 2026 a weak time, with comparable sales guided flat.

th3.evidence: Lowe's started as a single North Carolina hardware store and grew into the number-two player in a large, mature market, not by dominating a small niche.

team.evidence: Marvin Ellison is an experienced retail operator who improved margins, but he is not a founder and the team is solid rather than world-class.

th5.evidence: Lowe's has strong distribution: about 1,759 stores, roughly 16 million customer transactions a week, online channels and, since 2025, FBM's branch network.

durable.evidence: The big-box home improvement duopoly has proven resilient to e-commerce because bulky goods, immediate needs and Pro services favour local stores.

th7.evidence: Lowe's strategy follows the same Pro and services opportunity that Home Depot is also pursuing; it is not a unique insight.

trend.evidence: Lowe's is not a leading beneficiary of AI, cloud or another platform shift; its main driver is the housing cycle.

dr1.evidence: FY2026 guidance was cut to the low end in August 2026 and adjusted EPS of about $12.25 is roughly flat with FY2025's $12.28.

dr2.evidence: Lower mortgage rates and the integration of FBM and ADG could make results look better in 18-24 months, but that depends on a housing recovery that is uncertain.

dr4.evidence: High mortgage rates and weak existing-home sales weigh on home improvement demand, and the company carries about $1.6B of annual net interest expense.

dr6.evidence: Possible catalysts include Federal Reserve rate cuts reviving housing turnover, FBM synergies, tariff refunds and the Nov 18, 2026 Q3 report.

dr7.evidence: Flat organic sales, falling margins and high leverage do not support a large, concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was 33.48% in FY2025, typical for a retailer and below what signals strong pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: FY2025 free cash flow of $7.65B is about a 6.9% yield on a market value near $110B, attractive for a stable business.

gb2.evidence: Trailing operating income of about $10.3B is roughly 7% of an enterprise value near $145B, reasonable but not cheap.

pa2.evidence: The slowdown is largely cyclical: high rates have depressed housing turnover and DIY projects, which should recover when rates fall.

pa4.evidence: The duopoly position and steady cash flow make permanent loss unlikely, but $37.6B of debt and acquisition risk raise downside.

wo1.evidence: Lowe's is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Lowe's product costs are not falling quickly with volume; tariffs have pushed some costs up.

wo3.evidence: Lowe's is a retailer and distributor, not a combination of innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: The home improvement market grows with housing and the economy and will not be many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: Results depend on interest rates, the housing market, lumber prices and tariffs.

ns1.evidence: Lowe's does not visibly pass scale savings to customers; it declined to match rivals' price cuts in July 2026 and focuses on margin.

ns4.evidence: Pro distribution acquisitions may strengthen Lowe's position, but Home Depot is investing similarly at larger scale.

va2.evidence: Fixing and improving homes is a large, recurring need, but it is well served by many competitors.

tn1.evidence: Lowe's sells into the cyclical housing market, not a secular trend like AI, energy or robotics.

tn2.evidence: The market sees Lowe's as a home improvement retailer, which is what it is; the FBM and ADG deals add distribution but do not change its identity.

tn3.evidence: Lowe's is a large US company, but home improvement is seasonal (spring outdoor sales) and cyclical.

tn4.evidence: It is profitable ($6.7B in FY2025), but revenue fell in FY2023 and FY2024 and debt ($37.6B) far exceeds cash ($3.4B).

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow has been positive, but debt has far exceeded cash in every recent quarter ($37.6B vs $3.4B at July 31, 2026).

tn6.evidence: FY2025 revenue grew 3.1%, and FY2026 guidance implies about 6.6% growth, mostly from acquisitions.

tn7.evidence: FY2025 revenue growth of 3.1% plus a free-cash-flow margin of 8.9% totals about 12, far below 40.

tn8.evidence: In FY2025 revenue grew 3.1% while SG&A plus depreciation rose 7.6% (from $17.41B to $18.73B).

tn9.evidence: It hits instant kills: debt exceeds cash, operating margin was 11.77% (below 20%), and revenue growth is below 10%.

tn10.evidence: No major legal threat is evident, but US tariff policy directly affects its product costs and pricing.

tn11.evidence: Lowe's provides home improvement products and installation that help homeowners and contractors repair and improve homes, charging retail and service prices; customers choose it for convenience, assortment and appliances.

tn13.evidence: Total about 50: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 5, short interest 10 (1.9%), institutional ownership 10 (about 80%), revenue faster than expenses 0, 5-year return vs S&P 0, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 0, culture 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue fell in FY2023 and FY2024, operating margin declined from 13.38% (FY2023) to 11.77% (FY2025), and debt exceeded cash every year.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage of about 7.2x passes and the current ratio is about 1.1, but total liabilities ($64.1B at Jan 30, 2026) exceed assets excluding goodwill ($50.2B) and equity is negative.

tn18.evidence: Ellison has run Lowe's since 2018 and lifted margins and EPS, but he is not a founder, has less than 10 years in the role, and no open-market share purchases were found.

tn20.evidence: Lowe's beat adjusted EPS consensus in Q4 FY2025 ($1.98 vs $1.95) and Q2 FY2026 ($4.40 vs $4.22), but Q2 sales missed and guidance was lowered.

tn21.evidence: Operating margin has declined three years in a row (13.38% to 11.77%) and it made two large acquisitions ($8.8B FBM and ~$1.3B ADG) in 2025.

tn22.evidence: Lowe's has large revenue, steady profits and does not sell shares to raise cash; it avoids the hype trap.

tn24.evidence: The roughly 6-7% free-cash-flow yield implies only low-single-digit growth, close to what Lowe's delivers organically (comparable sales near flat) plus acquisitions.

tn25.evidence: Using 3-year average FCF margin (8.4%) and growth (negative, trimmed to about zero), a 12% discount rate and 4% terminal growth, minus $34B net debt, gives roughly $90 a share, well below $197.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E of about 16 on adjusted EPS of $12.31 against about 5.6% EPS growth gives a PEG near 3, above 1, though the P/E is below Home Depot's.
